title: How Leaders Talk About AI Can Influence Acceptance or Resistance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Draws on Harvard Business School research covering over 2,300 workers to argue that resistance to AI splits into performance-based objections (doubts about reliability) and principle-based ones (moral discomfort with AI replacing human judgment in caregiving, education, or relationships). The piece's key claim is that leaders unintentionally trigger the second, harder-to-move objection by framing AI adoption around 'efficiency' and 'cost savings,' language that team members hear as code for replacement. It cites the study's finding that 94 percent of respondents support AI as an augmentation tool, contrasted with strong resistance to AI framed as substitution. The prescription is a vocabulary swap -- drop 'efficiency,' 'automation,' and 'substitute' in favor of language describing what people can now do that they couldn't before.
points: AI resistance splits into performance-based doubts (will it work well enough) and principle-based objections (moral discomfort with AI replacing human roles), and only the first fades as the technology improves.
Leaders inadvertently harden resistance by leading with 'efficiency and cost savings' language, which employees decode as 'replacement' regardless of intent.
94 percent of surveyed workers support AI as an augmentation tool, showing the resistance is to substitution framing, not to AI adoption itself.
quotes: According to the study of over 2,300 workers, people resist AI for two types of reasons: performance-based and principle-based.
Some team members have a “moral repugnance” toward AI, viewing the use of the tools in some contexts as inherently wrong, regardless of how capable or cost-effective the technology is.
When leaders frame AI in terms of “efficiency gains and cost savings,” team members hear “replacement.” It doesn’t matter if that’s not the intent. The language does the work.
The HBS study found 94 percent of the respondents support AI as a tool that helps humans do their jobs better.
The distinction between “AI will handle this for you” and “AI will help you do this better” may sound like semantics, but it is huge.
Get the framing wrong, and you’ll spend months managing resistance that better language would have prevented.
